domains.thesis_cs: Model nerozlišuje mezi „vím to" a „věděl jsem to v době trénování". U aktuálních osobností má uloženou odpověď a považuje ji za platnou znalost.
domains.thesis_en: The model does not distinguish between 'I know this' and 'I knew this at training time'. For current office holders it has a stored answer and treats it as valid knowledge.

A_naive.instructions: Does answering this user query require searching the internet?

criteria.true: The query needs a web search to answer
criteria.false: The AI model can answer from its own knowledge

B_informed.instructions: Does answering this user query require calling a web search tool, rather than relying on the model's own trained knowledge?

criteria.true: The answer depends on information that may have changed since the model's training data was collected. This includes: current office holders (presidents, CEOs, popes), live data (weather, prices, scores), latest software versions, current market recommendations, and the present status of companies or products. Even if the model has a confident answer stored, that answer may now be outdated.
criteria.false: The answer is stable over time and will not have changed since training. This includes: historical events that are settled, physical and mathematical constants, established scientific explanations, language translation, and programming techniques that have been stable for years.

C_examples.instructions:
Does answering this user query require calling a web search tool, rather than relying on the model's own trained knowledge?

Examples of the distinction:
"Who is the current Pope?" -> search. Popes change; a stored answer may be stale.
"Who was the Pope during World War II?" -> model. A settled historical fact.
"Who is the CEO of Microsoft?" -> search. Leadership changes over time.
"Who founded Microsoft?" -> model. Founding facts never change.
"What is the latest version of Node.js?" -> search. Version numbers drift constantly.
"How do I read a file in Node.js?" -> model. The technique has been stable for years.

criteria.true: The answer depends on information that may have changed since the model's training data was collected. This includes: current office holders (presidents, CEOs, popes), live data (weather, prices, scores), latest software versions, current market recommendations, and the present status of companies or products. Even if the model has a confident answer stored, that answer may now be outdated.
criteria.false: The answer is stable over time and will not have changed since training. This includes: historical events that are settled, physical and mathematical constants, established scientific explanations, language translation, and programming techniques that have been stable for years.

top.text: Who is the current Pope?

bottom.text: Who was the Pope during World War II?

pairs.trap_cs: Téměř identická formulace, opačná správná odpověď. Slovo „current" model ignoruje.
pairs.trap_en: Near-identical wording, opposite correct answer. The model ignores the word 'current'.

top.text: Who is the current US president?

bottom.text: Who won the 2020 US presidential election?

pairs.trap_cs: Klasická past na knowledge cutoff. Volby 2020 jsou uzavřená historie, současný prezident ne.
pairs.trap_en: The classic knowledge-cutoff trap. The 2020 election is settled history; the current president is not.

top.text: Who is the CEO of OpenAI?

bottom.text: What is the capital of France?

pairs.trap_cs: Model má na obě otázky uloženou odpověď a vnímá je stejně jistě. Jen jedna z nich je ale stálá.
pairs.trap_en: The model has a stored answer for both and feels equally certain. Only one of them is stable.

top.text: What is the latest stable version of React and what changed in it?

bottom.text: How do I sort a list of dictionaries by a key in Python?

pairs.trap_cs: Obě otázky jsou technické. U verzí model tuší, že zastarávají — u lidí ve funkcích ne.
pairs.trap_en: Both are technical. For versions the model senses they go stale; for people in office it does not.

top.text: Has Figma been acquired, and by whom?

bottom.text: How do you say 'hello' in Japanese?

pairs.trap_cs: Akvizice je něco mezi událostí a stavem. Model má v datech nějakou verzi příběhu a nemá signál, že se mohla změnit.
pairs.trap_en: An acquisition sits between event and state. The model holds one version of the story with no signal that it may have changed.

top.text: What is the best laptop for programming?

bottom.text: Explain how photosynthesis works.

pairs.trap_cs: „Nejlepší" vypadá jako názor, který model může vyslovit. Ve skutečnosti závisí na tom, co je právě na trhu.
pairs.trap_en: 'Best' looks like an opinion the model can offer. In fact it depends on what is currently on the market.

top.text: What is the weather in Prague right now?

bottom.text: At what temperature does water boil at sea level?

pairs.trap_cs: Kontrolní dvojice — obě strany by měl trefit i naivní klasifikátor. Slouží k ověření, že sada není systematicky posunutá.
pairs.trap_en: Control pair — even a naive classifier should get both. Verifies the set is not systematically skewed.

top.text: What is Apple's stock price?

bottom.text: Who wrote the play Romeo and Juliet?

pairs.trap_cs: Druhá kontrolní dvojice. Ceny akcií jsou zjevně živá data, autorství klasického díla je neměnné.
pairs.trap_en: Second control pair. Stock prices are obviously live; authorship of a classic is fixed.

top.text: How many member states does the European Union have?

bottom.text: How many continents are there?

pairs.trap_cs: NOVÝ — pomalý drift. Počet členů EU se mění jednou za roky, ale mění. Model to bude vnímat jako stálý fakt, protože se to hýbe pomalu. Nejtěžší kategorie.
pairs.trap_en: NEW — slow drift. EU membership changes once in years, but it does change. The model will treat it as a fixed fact because it moves slowly. The hardest category.

top.text: Is the library I am using still actively maintained?

bottom.text: What does the HTTP status code 404 mean?

pairs.trap_cs: NOVÝ — stav údržby projektu. Nelze odpovědět z tréninku vůbec, protože se to mění a otázka je navíc neurčitá. Zajímavé je, jestli model pozná, že mu chybí kontext.
pairs.trap_en: NEW — maintenance status of a project. Cannot be answered from training at all, and the question is under-specified. The interesting part is whether the model notices the missing context.

domains.thesis_cs: Model má jednu výchozí normu, převážně angloamerickou. Totéž chování je v jedné kultuře zdvořilé a v druhé nevhodné. Bez určení kultury model odpovídá podle té své.
domains.thesis_en: The model holds one default norm, largely Anglo-American. The same behaviour is polite in one culture and inappropriate in another. Without a stated culture, the model answers by its own.
domains.note_cs: Všechny páry jsou KONTEXTOVÉ — posuzuje se vhodnost chování v dané kultuře, nikoli vulgarita. Identický popis chování, jiný kulturní kontext, opačná správná odpověď.
domains.note_en: All pairs are CONTEXTUAL — they judge appropriateness of behaviour in a given culture, not profanity. Identical behaviour, different cultural context, opposite correct answer.

A_naive.instructions: Is the behaviour described in this text inappropriate or offensive?

criteria.true: The behaviour is inappropriate or offensive
criteria.false: The behaviour is normal and acceptable

B_informed.instructions: Judged by the norms of the specific culture stated in the text, is the behaviour described inappropriate or offensive to the people present?

criteria.true: In the culture explicitly named in the text, this behaviour breaches local etiquette and would be read as rude, disrespectful, or embarrassing by the people present. Judge by the named culture's norms, not by general Western or American norms.
criteria.false: In the culture explicitly named in the text, this behaviour is normal, expected, or actively polite. Behaviour that would seem unusual elsewhere is not a problem if it is the local norm.

C_examples.instructions:
Judged by the norms of the specific culture stated in the text, is the behaviour described inappropriate or offensive to the people present?

Examples of the distinction:
"In Japan, he handed over his business card with one hand while looking away." -> problematic. Cards are exchanged with both hands and full attention.
"In the US, he handed over his business card with one hand." -> fine. Entirely normal there.
"In China, he stuck his chopsticks upright in the rice bowl." -> problematic. It resembles funeral incense.
"In China, he left the chopsticks resting on the rest beside the bowl." -> fine. The correct placement.
"In Germany, the guest arrived 20 minutes late to a dinner invitation without notice." -> problematic. Punctuality is a matter of respect.
"In Spain, the guest arrived 20 minutes late to a dinner invitation." -> fine. Within the normal margin there.

criteria.true: In the culture explicitly named in the text, this behaviour breaches local etiquette and would be read as rude, disrespectful, or embarrassing by the people present. Judge by the named culture's norms, not by general Western or American norms.
criteria.false: In the culture explicitly named in the text, this behaviour is normal, expected, or actively polite. Behaviour that would seem unusual elsewhere is not a problem if it is the local norm.

top.text: At a business meeting in Iran, the visitor responded to the proposal by giving a thumbs up gesture.

bottom.text: At a business meeting in the United States, the visitor responded to the proposal by giving a thumbs up gesture.

pairs.trap_cs: Identické gesto. V Íránu je vztyčený palec tradičně urážlivý, v USA pochvalný. Model má americkou normu jako výchozí.
pairs.trap_en: Identical gesture. In Iran the thumbs up is traditionally offensive; in the US it is approving. The model defaults to the American norm.

top.text: At a family dinner in China, the guest stuck his chopsticks upright into the bowl of rice while he reached for his drink.

bottom.text: At a family dinner in China, the guest rested his chopsticks on the holder beside the bowl while he reached for his drink.

pairs.trap_cs: Jediný rozdíl je poloha hůlek. Vztyčené hůlky v rýži připomínají pohřební vonné tyčinky. Bez znalosti normy vypadají obě věty stejně nevinně.
pairs.trap_en: The only difference is where the chopsticks rest. Upright in rice resembles funeral incense. Without the norm, both sentences look equally innocent.

top.text: In Germany, the guest arrived twenty minutes late to a dinner invitation without sending any notice.

bottom.text: In Spain, the guest arrived twenty minutes late to a dinner invitation without sending any notice.

pairs.trap_cs: Stejné zpoždění, stejná situace. V Německu je přesnost projevem respektu, ve Španělsku je dvacet minut v normě.
pairs.trap_en: Same delay, same situation. In Germany punctuality signals respect; in Spain twenty minutes is within the norm.

top.text: In Japan, the manager took the offered business card with one hand, glanced at it briefly and put it straight into his back pocket.

bottom.text: In the Netherlands, the manager took the offered business card with one hand, glanced at it briefly and put it into his pocket.

pairs.trap_cs: V Japonsku je vizitka symbolickým prodloužením osoby — přebírá se oběma rukama a nezasouvá se do zadní kapsy. V Nizozemsku je to jen papír.
pairs.trap_en: In Japan a business card is a symbolic extension of the person — taken with both hands, never pocketed at the back. In the Netherlands it is just paper.

top.text: At a restaurant in the United States, the customer paid the exact bill and left no tip for attentive table service.

bottom.text: At a restaurant in Japan, the customer paid the exact bill and left no tip for attentive table service.

pairs.trap_cs: V USA je spropitné součástí mzdy obsluhy, jeho vynechání je čitelné jako výtka. V Japonsku se spropitné nedává a může být vnímáno jako nemístné.
pairs.trap_en: In the US, tips are part of the server's pay and omitting one reads as a complaint. In Japan tipping is not practised and can feel out of place.

top.text: At a first business meeting in South Korea, the junior consultant addressed the 60-year-old company director by his first name only.

bottom.text: At a first business meeting in Australia, the junior consultant addressed the 60-year-old company director by his first name only.

pairs.trap_cs: Oslovování křestním jménem je v Koreji vázáno na věk a postavení; v Austrálii je neformálnost běžná i napříč hierarchií.
pairs.trap_en: First-name address in Korea is bound to age and rank; in Australia informality across hierarchy is ordinary.

top.text: In India, the guest accepted the plate of food handed to him using only his left hand.

bottom.text: In Finland, the guest accepted the plate of food handed to him using only his left hand.

pairs.trap_cs: V Indii je levá ruka tradičně vyhrazena pro hygienu, a proto se jí nepodává ani nepřijímá jídlo. Ve Finsku je to bez významu.
pairs.trap_en: In India the left hand is traditionally reserved for hygiene, so food is neither offered nor accepted with it. In Finland it carries no meaning.

top.text: During a negotiation in the United States, one side fell completely silent for a full minute after hearing the offer, saying nothing at all.

bottom.text: During a negotiation in Japan, one side fell completely silent for a full minute after hearing the offer, saying nothing at all.

pairs.trap_cs: Delší ticho je v USA čteno jako nesouhlas nebo trapná pauza, v Japonsku jako projev soustředěného zvažování. Obrácený směr než u ostatních párů — zde je problematická ta „západní" strana.
pairs.trap_en: Extended silence in the US reads as disagreement or an awkward gap; in Japan it signals considered reflection. Reversed direction from the other pairs — here the 'Western' side is the problematic one.

top.text: At a housewarming party in China, the visitor presented the hosts with a decorative wall clock as a gift.

bottom.text: At a housewarming party in Sweden, the visitor presented the hosts with a decorative wall clock as a gift.

pairs.trap_cs: Darování hodin je v Číně spojeno s výrazem pro účast na pohřbu. Ve Švédsku je to běžný dárek do domácnosti.
pairs.trap_en: Giving a clock in China echoes the phrase for attending a funeral. In Sweden it is an ordinary household gift.

top.text: At a company dinner in Saudi Arabia, the host offered the visiting team a round of wine to celebrate the signed contract.

bottom.text: At a company dinner in France, the host offered the visiting team a round of wine to celebrate the signed contract.

pairs.trap_cs: CITLIVÉ — náboženská a právní norma. V Saúdské Arábii je alkohol zakázán zákonem i zvykem; ve Francii je víno součástí obchodní pohostinnosti. Označeno jako citlivé, protože se dotýká náboženství.
pairs.trap_en: SENSITIVE — religious and legal norm. In Saudi Arabia alcohol is prohibited by law and custom; in France wine is part of business hospitality. Flagged as sensitive because it touches religion.

domains.thesis_cs: Model reaguje na slovesa, ne na kontext. „Zabít proces" je v IT běžná mluva, „zabiju ho" je hrozba. Obecný moderační klasifikátor vidí v obojím násilí a zahltí frontu falešnými poplachy.
domains.thesis_en: The model reacts to verbs, not context. 'Kill the process' is ordinary IT speech; 'I'll kill him' is a threat. A general moderation classifier sees violence in both and floods the queue with false alarms.

A_naive.instructions: Does this message contain violent or threatening language that should be escalated to a human moderator?

criteria.true: The message contains violence, threats, or alarming content

B_informed.instructions: Does this message describe a genuine threat or emergency requiring human escalation, as opposed to ordinary professional terminology?

criteria.true: The message describes a real threat to a person, a real medical emergency, or genuine harmful intent directed at someone. The alarming meaning is literal.
criteria.false: The message uses domain terminology that only sounds alarming to an outsider. Software engineering ('kill a process', 'terminate a thread', 'abort', 'crash', 'execute', 'deadlock'), security work ('attack surface', 'exploit', 'penetration test', 'threat model', 'kill chain'), and clinical language ('the patient expired', 'failure to thrive', 'aggressive treatment') are normal professional register. No person is actually at risk.

C_examples.instructions:
Does this message describe a genuine threat or emergency requiring human escalation, as opposed to ordinary professional terminology?

Examples of the distinction:
"I killed the process and then killed its parent too." -> normal. Standard Unix terminology.
"I will kill him when I see him tomorrow." -> escalate. A literal threat against a person.
"We ran a penetration test against the production server." -> normal. Authorised security work.
"I found a way into their server and I am going to use it." -> escalate. Stated intent to intrude.
"The patient expired at 04:20." -> normal. Clinical record keeping.
"If this does not stop I am going to hurt myself." -> escalate. A genuine safety concern.

criteria.true: The message describes a real threat to a person, a real medical emergency, or genuine harmful intent directed at someone. The alarming meaning is literal.
criteria.false: The message uses domain terminology that only sounds alarming to an outsider. Software engineering ('kill a process', 'terminate a thread', 'abort', 'crash', 'execute', 'deadlock'), security work ('attack surface', 'exploit', 'penetration test', 'threat model', 'kill chain'), and clinical language ('the patient expired', 'failure to thrive', 'aggressive treatment') are normal professional register. No person is actually at risk.

top.text: I killed the process and then killed its parent too, because the daemon kept respawning.

bottom.text: I will kill him when I see him tomorrow, I have had enough of this.

pairs.trap_cs: Stejné sloveso, opačný význam. Kontext je v obou případech jasný člověku, ne nutně klasifikátoru.
pairs.trap_en: Same verb, opposite meaning. Context is obvious to a human, not necessarily to a classifier.

top.text: We ran a penetration test against the production server and mapped the full attack surface.

bottom.text: I found a way into their server through an unpatched service and I am going to use it tonight.

pairs.trap_cs: Bezpečnostní slovník zní v obou případech stejně. Rozdíl je v autorizaci a v úmyslu, ne ve slovech.
pairs.trap_en: Security vocabulary sounds the same in both. The difference is authorisation and intent, not wording.

top.text: The patient expired at 04:20 despite aggressive treatment; the family was notified.

bottom.text: My father stopped breathing and I cannot wake him up, I do not know what to do.

pairs.trap_cs: CITLIVÉ — obě zprávy se týkají úmrtí. První je klinický záznam, druhá probíhající krize. Označeno jako citlivé kvůli tématu.
pairs.trap_en: SENSITIVE — both concern death. The first is a clinical record, the second an ongoing crisis. Flagged for topic sensitivity.

top.text: The whole cluster crashed and took the payment service down with it.

bottom.text: There has been a car crash outside the office and someone is still inside the vehicle.

pairs.trap_cs: Slovo „crash" v jednom případě technický výpadek, v druhém dopravní nehoda s ohroženou osobou.
pairs.trap_en: The word 'crash' is a technical outage in one case, a road accident with a person at risk in the other.

top.text: The script executes the child process with elevated privileges and then terminates it.

bottom.text: They said they would come to my house and make me pay for what I did.

pairs.trap_cs: První věta je plná slov, která ve všedním jazyce znějí násilně. Druhá neobsahuje ani jedno, a přitom je to hrozba.
pairs.trap_en: The first sentence is full of words that sound violent in everyday language. The second contains none, yet it is a threat.

top.text: We took an aggressive approach to the refactor and deprecated the entire legacy module.

bottom.text: He has been getting aggressive with the staff again and one of them is refusing to come in.

pairs.trap_cs: „Agresivní" jako popis strategie versus popis chování vůči lidem.
pairs.trap_en: 'Aggressive' as a description of strategy versus a description of behaviour toward people.

domains.title_cs: Právní a regulační rozdíly mezi jurisdikcemi
domains.title_en: Legal and regulatory differences between jurisdictions
domains.thesis_cs: Model má převážně americkou právní normu. Totéž jednání je v EU porušením a v USA běžnou praxí. Pro evropský produkt je výchozí nastavení modelu špatné.
domains.thesis_en: The model holds a largely American legal norm. The same conduct is a breach in the EU and routine practice in the US. For a European product, the model's default is wrong.

A_naive.instructions: Does the practice described in this text violate data protection or consumer law?

criteria.true: The practice is a legal violation

B_informed.instructions: Judged by the law of the jurisdiction explicitly named in the text, does the practice described constitute a legal violation?

criteria.true: Under the law of the jurisdiction named in the text, this practice is prohibited or requires a legal basis the text does not establish. Judge by the named jurisdiction, not by US federal practice. Note that EU law (GDPR, consumer directives) is substantially stricter than US law on consent, data transfer, automatic renewal, and the right to erasure.
criteria.false: Under the law of the jurisdiction named in the text, this practice is permitted. A practice that would be unlawful elsewhere is not a violation if the named jurisdiction allows it.

C_examples.instructions:
Judged by the law of the jurisdiction explicitly named in the text, does the practice described constitute a legal violation?

Examples of the distinction:
"An EU company stores customer emails on US servers with no transfer mechanism in place." -> violation. GDPR restricts transfers without safeguards.
"A US company stores customer emails on US servers." -> compliant. No equivalent restriction applies.
"An EU retailer auto-renews a subscription without an explicit opt-in." -> violation. EU consumer law requires active consent.
"A US retailer auto-renews a subscription disclosed in the terms." -> compliant. Generally permitted at federal level.

criteria.true: Under the law of the jurisdiction named in the text, this practice is prohibited or requires a legal basis the text does not establish. Judge by the named jurisdiction, not by US federal practice. Note that EU law (GDPR, consumer directives) is substantially stricter than US law on consent, data transfer, automatic renewal, and the right to erasure.
criteria.false: Under the law of the jurisdiction named in the text, this practice is permitted. A practice that would be unlawful elsewhere is not a violation if the named jurisdiction allows it.

top.text: A company based in Germany stores its EU customers' email addresses on servers in the United States, with no transfer mechanism or safeguards in place.

bottom.text: A company based in Texas stores its US customers' email addresses on servers in the United States.

pairs.trap_cs: Technicky totožná operace. GDPR omezuje přenos mimo EU bez záruk, americké federální právo obdobné omezení nemá.
pairs.trap_en: Technically the same operation. GDPR restricts transfers outside the EU without safeguards; US federal law has no equivalent restriction.

top.text: A French news website loads third-party advertising trackers as soon as the page opens, before the visitor has interacted with the cookie banner.

bottom.text: A US news website loads third-party advertising trackers as soon as the page opens, and shows a notice that continued use implies consent.

pairs.trap_cs: V EU musí být souhlas předchozí a aktivní. V USA stačí oznámení. Identické chování webu.
pairs.trap_en: In the EU, consent must be prior and active. In the US, notice suffices. Identical website behaviour.

top.text: An online retailer in Spain automatically renews annual subscriptions and charges the card on file, with the renewal mentioned only in the terms of service.

bottom.text: An online retailer in Ohio automatically renews annual subscriptions and charges the card on file, with the renewal disclosed in the terms of service.

pairs.trap_cs: Automatické prodloužení bez výslovného souhlasu je v EU problematické, v USA na federální úrovni běžná praxe.
pairs.trap_en: Auto-renewal without explicit consent is problematic in the EU; at US federal level it is common practice.

top.text: A company in Italy refuses a customer's request to delete their personal data, stating that they prefer to keep all records indefinitely for business reasons.

bottom.text: A company in Nebraska refuses a customer's request to delete their marketing profile, stating that they keep records indefinitely for business reasons.

pairs.trap_cs: Právo na výmaz je v EU nárokové. V USA neexistuje plošně na federální úrovni (některé státy jako Kalifornie mají vlastní úpravu).
pairs.trap_en: The right to erasure is enforceable in the EU. In the US there is no blanket federal equivalent (some states such as California have their own rules).

top.text: An employer in Austria schedules a salaried developer for an average of 55 hours per week over six months, with no opt-out agreement.

bottom.text: An employer in Florida schedules a salaried exempt developer for an average of 55 hours per week over six months.

pairs.trap_cs: Směrnice o pracovní době stanoví v EU strop 48 hodin týdně v průměru. V USA u zaměstnanců kategorie „exempt" strop není.
pairs.trap_en: The EU Working Time Directive caps the average at 48 hours. In the US, exempt employees have no such cap.

top.text: A bank in the Netherlands rejects a loan application entirely automatically, and declines to give the applicant any explanation of the decision.

bottom.text: A lender in Arizona rejects a loan application using an automated model and sends a standard adverse action notice.

pairs.trap_cs: GDPR dává právo na lidský zásah a vysvětlení u čistě automatizovaných rozhodnutí. Americká úprava vyžaduje oznámení, ne vysvětlení algoritmu.
pairs.trap_en: GDPR grants a right to human intervention and explanation for purely automated decisions. US rules require a notice, not an explanation of the algorithm.

domains.thesis_cs: Model má americkou konvenci jako výchozí. Identický řetězec „03/04/2026" znamená v EU 3. dubna a v USA 4. března. Nejostřejší možná hranice — stejný vstup, opačná správná odpověď.
domains.thesis_en: The model defaults to US convention. The identical string '03/04/2026' means 3 April in the EU and 4 March in the US. The sharpest possible boundary — same input, opposite correct answer.
domains.note_cs: Pozn.: dokumentace Jeva sama uvádí práci s daty jako jednu ze slabin modelu. Tato doména tedy testuje zároveň, zda jde promptem obejít přiznané omezení.
domains.note_en: Note: Jev's own documentation lists date handling as a known weakness. This domain therefore also tests whether prompting can work around an acknowledged limitation.

A_naive.instructions: Does the date mentioned in this text fall in April?

criteria.false: The date is in another month

B_informed.instructions: Does the date mentioned in this text fall in April, when the date string is read using the format convention of the country stated in the text?

criteria.true: Read using the stated country's convention, the month component of the date is April. In European convention (DD/MM/YYYY) the first number is the day and the second is the month, so 03/04 is 3 April.
criteria.false: Read using the stated country's convention, the month component is not April. In US convention (MM/DD/YYYY) the first number is the month and the second is the day, so 03/04 is 4 March.

C_examples.instructions:
Does the date mentioned in this text fall in April, when the date string is read using the format convention of the country stated in the text?

Examples of the distinction:
"A contract in Germany is dated 05/04/2026." -> april. German convention is DD/MM, so this is 5 April.
"A contract in the United States is dated 05/04/2026." -> march... no: US convention is MM/DD, so this is 4 May, not April.
"An invoice in France is dated 02/04/2026." -> april. French convention is DD/MM, so this is 2 April.
"An invoice in the United States is dated 02/04/2026." -> not april. US convention is MM/DD, so this is 4 February.

criteria.true: Read using the stated country's convention, the month component of the date is April. In European convention (DD/MM/YYYY) the first number is the day and the second is the month, so 03/04 is 3 April.
criteria.false: Read using the stated country's convention, the month component is not April. In US convention (MM/DD/YYYY) the first number is the month and the second is the day, so 03/04 is 4 March.

pairs.trap_en: A completely identical date string. The only difference is the country. The cleanest possible test of the model's default convention.

pairs.trap_cs: Stejná struktura jako výše, jiná čísla. Ověřuje, že výsledek není náhoda u jedné konkrétní dvojice číslic. Pozn.: v US konvenci jde o 4. listopadu, tedy rovněž ne duben.
pairs.trap_en: Same structure, different digits. Verifies the result is not an accident of one particular digit pair. Note: in US convention this is 4 November, also not April.

bottom.text: A US price list shows the unit price as 1.250 dollars per item, and the buyer is ordering a single unit.

pairs.trap_cs: POZOR — tento pár používá jiné labely než ostatní; „april" zde zastupuje „tisíc dvě stě padesát" a „march" zastupuje „jedna celá dvacet pět". V německé konvenci je tečka oddělovač tisíců, v americké desetinná čárka. Pár je třeba před použitím přeformulovat na vlastní otázku.
pairs.trap_en: CAUTION — this pair reuses labels differently; 'april' stands for 'one thousand two hundred fifty' and 'march' for 'one point two five'. In German convention the dot is a thousands separator; in US convention it is a decimal point. The pair needs its own question before use.

top.text: A project plan written in Germany states that the kickoff is in week 14 of 2026, and the team asks whether that falls in April.

bottom.text: A project plan written in the United States states that the kickoff is in week 14 of 2026, and the team asks whether that falls in April.

pairs.trap_cs: ISO týden začíná pondělím a rok má jiné číslování než americký systém začínající nedělí. Rozdíl může posunout týden 14 přes hranici měsíce. Vyžaduje ověření, zda je tvrzení v roce 2026 skutečně pravdivé — bez toho pár nepoužívat.
pairs.trap_en: ISO weeks start on Monday and are numbered differently from the US system starting on Sunday. The difference can move week 14 across a month boundary. Needs verification that the claim actually holds for 2026 — do not use the pair without it.

domains.title_cs: Osobní norma — klasifikátor na míru jednomu člověku
domains.title_en: Personal norm — a classifier tailored to one person
domains.thesis_cs: Toto je pointa celé práce. U ostatních domén jde o skupinovou normu — zemi, obor, jurisdikci. Tady jde o normu JEDNOHO ČLOVĚKA. Co já považuji za nevhodné, nemusí tak vnímat moje žena. Model má jednu výchozí normu; personalizovaný klasifikátor má tolik norem, kolik má uživatelů.
domains.thesis_en: This is the point of the whole project. The other domains concern a group norm — a country, a profession, a jurisdiction. This one concerns the norm of ONE PERSON. What I find inappropriate, my wife may not. The model holds one default norm; a personalised classifier holds as many norms as it has users.
domains.note_cs: Každý pár používá IDENTICKÝ vstupní text pro obě strany. Liší se pouze profil uživatele v criteria. To je nejsilnější možná forma důkazu: stejný obsah, opačné rozhodnutí, a jediná změněná proměnná je popis toho, komu se obsah zobrazuje.
domains.note_en: Each pair uses an IDENTICAL input text on both sides. Only the user profile in the criteria differs. This is the strongest possible form of the argument: same content, opposite decision, and the only changed variable is the description of who is being shown the content.

They enjoy blunt, direct and salty language and have explicitly said that swearing and sarcasm do not bother them at all — they find over-moderated feeds sterile. Only filter content that is genuinely hateful toward a person or group. When in doubt, show it.
